title: SELECT * Triggers a Key Lookup
description: SELECT * forces a Key Lookup back to the table for columns the index doesn't hold; select only what you need (or cover the index) to drop the lookup. Why it matters: SELECT * is one of the most widespread habits in real codebases, and this is precisely why it quietly costs more than it looks like it should.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson is about a habit almost every developer picks up early — writing `SELECT *` — and why it can quietly sabotage an otherwise well-indexed query. You'll learn about a plan operator called a **Key Lookup**, which is the tax you pay for asking for more columns than your index actually stores.

Why does this happen? An index doesn't have to contain every column in the table — usually it only stores the columns useful for filtering, plus a pointer back to the full row. If your query filters on `CustomerId` (which the index covers) but also asks for `Notes` (which the index does *not* store), SQL Server has to do two jobs: first, seek the index to find the matching rows quickly; second, for *each* of those rows, hop over to the full table to fetch the missing column.

Picture a library card catalog: it tells you the author, title, and which shelf a book is on — but not the book's full text. If you want the full text, you still have to walk to the shelf and pull the physical book for every single card you found. That "walk to the shelf" step, repeated per matching row, is the Key Lookup — and if you're matching thousands of rows, that's thousands of extra trips. `SELECT *` almost always asks for columns beyond what the index stores, forcing this lookup. The fix is to either select only the columns you actually need, or extend the index to include them.

## Scenario
`SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 777` seeks the index on `CustomerId` but the plan also shows a **Key Lookup** and **Nested Loops** — extra work for every matching row.

## Why it's slow
The index `IX_Orders_Customer` contains `CustomerId` plus the common columns `OrderDate` and `Status`. But `SELECT *` also asks for `Notes`, which is **not** in the index. So for each matching row SQL Server does a **Key Lookup** back into the clustered index to fetch `Notes`. Lookups are random reads and, at higher row counts, can flip the optimizer to a full scan.

## What to look for
- A **Nested Loops** join feeding a lookup back into the clustered index (shown as a *Key Lookup* or a *Clustered Index Seek*) hanging off an otherwise efficient Index Seek.

## The concept
Ask only for the columns you actually need. If the query selects just the columns the index already covers (`OrderId`, `CustomerId`, `OrderDate`, `Status`), the seek is **covering** and the Key Lookup disappears. `SELECT *` is a habit that quietly defeats covering indexes — name your columns.
hints: The seek is fine — what is the Key Lookup fetching?
SELECT * asks for Notes, which isn't in the index, so each row needs a lookup.
Select only covered columns: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Status FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 777;
